# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is a strong follow-up. It does what the earlier critiques asked for: a registered mediation test, an independent hours measure, a two-year horizon, baseline meeting data, and an honest account of the counter arm's termination. Its rebuttals of both the "entirely an artifact" claim and the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim mostly hold. The main problems are an unexamined threat to the decay estimate (the control offices changed their own practices), ambiguity about what the log-hours measure captures, a mediation analysis that claims more than seven treated offices can support, and labour cost, which is still missing for case-processing.

## Arithmetic checks

**These pass:**
- Output per hour, timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = **+9.8%**.
- Output per hour, logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = **+8.5%**.
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = **100%**.
- Halden continuers: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, so hours fell **13.4%**; 0.968 / 0.866 = **+11.8%** per hour.
- Counter-arm staffing: actual hours fell 17% and output per hour rose 6.7%, so restoring output needs 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) ≈ **+13% staff**. That is consistent with the county's 12%. The +9% cost-per-contact figure fits if staff costs are about three-quarters of total cost. Please state the basis.

**This one needs checking:**
- **The control meeting figures don't obviously reconcile.** The seven control offices averaged 7.2 → 7.0 hours of meetings. Two of them fell to 5.0 after their audit. For the average to reach 7.0, the other five must have *risen* from about 7.2 to about 7.8 hours. That may be true, but it should be stated. Otherwise, clarify whether the 7.0 figure excludes the two audit offices or comes from before month 15.

## What's done well

- The mediation analysis was registered before the 24-month outcomes were available, with the mediators and outcome pre-specified.
- It adds an hours measure that doesn't depend on self-reporting, and reports both measures side by side.
- It reports baseline meeting data (7.4 vs 7.2), which closes the gap in the nine-month exploratory analysis.
- It reports the counter arm's termination and its cost, and gives waiting times against control, not just before vs after for treated offices.
- It frames the Halden continuers properly as "survivors twice over" and an upper bound.
- It checks the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies and finds them all uncontrolled and based on scheduled hours. This confirms that the "no decay" claim rested on the weakest designs.
- The section on the control offices' meeting audit is appropriately hedged.

## Major issues

### 1. The control offices' meeting audit contaminates the decay estimate

The report treats the month-15 meeting audit as a side observation. It is also a contamination of the control arm.

- Two of the seven control offices raised their output per hour by about 4.1% from month 15 onward, without changing hours.
- That raises the control average by roughly 1.2 points (2/7 × 4.1%, if weighted equally) and narrows the treated–control gap by the same amount.
- So part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may reflect the control offices improving, not the treated offices' gain fading.

The fix is to re-estimate excluding the two audit offices, or with an indicator for after the audit. Please also report whether the audit was prompted by the nine-month report's public discussion of meetings. If it was, this is spillover from the trial itself, and it affects how decay is interpreted.

### 2. The summary compares different hours measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% uses timesheets and the 8.5% uses system logs. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**, as the body says.

The summary also says "the gain has therefore declined" as a statement of fact. The two confidence intervals (6.9 to 18.4 and 4.6 to 15.2) overlap almost entirely, and the decline itself isn't tested. The body's wording, "consistent with some fading", is the right one and should be used in the summary too, along with the caveat from issue 1.

### 3. What do "log hours" actually measure?

The log measure is described as "active log-in time on the case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases". If it counts only time spent on cases, it is not a measure of total working time, and this changes the interpretation in two ways.

- **Why logs fell less than timesheets.** This could mean unrecorded work, as the report concludes. It could also mean the treated offices moved time out of meetings and into casework, which raises case time relative to total hours.
- **Whether the mediation is coherent.** If the outcome is output per hour of *casework*, cutting meetings shouldn't mechanically raise it. Any effect would have to work through less fragmented time or better focus. If logs include all logged-in time, including during meetings, the interpretation is different.

Also: logs are new at follow-up, and the nine-month column is blank. Is there pre-period log data? Without it, the −11% isn't a difference-in-differences estimate.

### 4. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result

- **It isn't out-of-sample.** The registered test uses the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis. Registering at month 11 protects against choosing the specification after seeing the results. But it is a test on more months of data from the same offices, not a replication. "Supports" or "is consistent with" would be more accurate than "confirms".
- **The CI is probably too narrow.** The meeting changes vary across offices, so the effective sample is seven treated offices, not the office-months. A 95% CI of 28–66% for a mediated share from seven offices looks tight. Please report how standard errors were clustered and whether a small-cluster correction was used.
- **Mediators aren't randomised.** Offices that cut meetings most may also have stronger managers, which is a confounding path. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary and Section 5 ignore it.
- **Measurement precision differs between mediators.** Calendar-based meeting hours are measured far more precisely than a self-reported fatigue scale. Measurement error shrinks a mediator's apparent share, so the 47% vs 18% comparison is partly about how well each was measured. Fatigue's contribution may be understated.
- **Additivity.** The two mediators may be correlated, since fewer meetings could itself reduce fatigue. Were the shares estimated jointly? If not, they may not be additive.
- **Is there a fatigue baseline?** The 0.34 SD improvement relative to control needs a baseline fatigue measure. Was it collected before the trial?

### 5. Labour cost is still missing for case-processing

The report costs the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not the case-processing arm. That arm is the one continuing, and the one other employers would copy. Scheduled hours fell 20% but actual hours fell only 11–12%. If the extra 2.5–3 hours a week are paid overtime on top of unchanged salaries, cost per case has risen, possibly by more than 10%, while output per employee is down 3.4%. This was the main gap in the nine-month report and is now the main gap here. Was the overtime paid or taken as time off in lieu?

### 6. The Halden subset

- **"All with client-facing or coverage obligations" is a stretch.** The marketing agency reverted because of client deadlines. That is deadline-based work, which the meta-analysis classifies as discretionary, not coverage-bound. One of the three reversions therefore doesn't fit the coverage story. It should be reported as such, not grouped with the other two.
- **The hours baseline is borrowed.** The 40.3-hour baseline is the 27-organisation figure from the Varga & Holm re-analysis. The 11 continuing organisations should be compared with their own pre-pilot hours.
- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations didn't provide 24-month data and were plausibly the less successful ones. That makes the figures selected three times over, not twice: pilot completion, agreeing to provide data, and continuation.

## Minor points

- **Define the 24-month timepoint.** Is it the month-24 snapshot or an average over months 19–24? This matters for how the audit contamination enters.
- **Sick days and resignations still have no CIs.** Resignations also remain a raw treated vs control comparison, not a DiD. The question of whether sick days are mechanically lower because there are fewer scheduled days is still unaddressed.
- **Appeal-overturn rates are now more informative.** At 24 months, appeals on early-trial decisions have had time to resolve. It is worth saying so, since this answers the earlier concern about appeals lagging.
- **Declare interests and correct the record.** The authors are evaluating critiques of their own work, and Okafor co-authored the Halden pilot. That's appropriate, but it should be declared. The Halden authors should also take the opportunity to correct the pilot's account of attrition: the re-analysis found that seven of nine withdrawals came after the schedule began.

## Suggested revised summary sentences

> In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control was 9.8% at 24 months on timesheets (12.5% at nine months) and 8.5% on system logs. The decline is consistent with some fading of the initial effect, though part may reflect two control offices independently cutting meetings from month 15. A registered mediation analysis on the same offices is consistent with reduced meeting time accounting for roughly half of the per-hour gain, and reduced fatigue for a smaller share.

## Where the five documents now leave things

The five documents together support a fairly clear picture:

- **Discretionary work.** A per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists to two years in the one controlled long-run study. Output per employee falls slightly, by about 3%, and cost per unit probably rises unless the extra hours are unpaid.
- **Coverage-bound work.** Output per employee and service quality fall, and restoring service needs more staff at higher cost.
- **Mechanism.** Reorganisation, especially cutting meetings, appears to matter at least as much as rest.

The open policy question is the one the report itself raises: can the reorganisation gains be captured without cutting hours? A trial arm that reorganises work without reducing hours would answer it.
